facts.title: Discovered Twice, Named Once
facts.text: Vanadium was first spotted in 1801 by Spanish-Mexican mineralogist Andrés Manuel del Río, who called it 'erythronium' because its salts turned red on heating. He was wrongly convinced he had merely found impure chromium and withdrew his claim. The element was rediscovered in 1830 by Swedish chemist Nils Gabriel Sefström, who got the lasting credit.

facts.title: Named For A Norse Goddess
facts.text: Sefström named the element after Vanadís, another name for Freyja, the Norse goddess of beauty and fertility. The choice honors vanadium's strikingly beautiful, multicolored compounds. It is one of the few elements named after a figure from Norse mythology rather than Greek or Roman.

facts.title: A Rainbow In A Test Tube
facts.text: Vanadium is famous for forming ions in four common oxidation states, each with its own vivid color: +2 is violet, +3 is green, +4 is blue, and +5 is yellow. Chemistry teachers reduce a yellow vanadium(V) solution with zinc to watch it cascade through blue, green, and violet. This makes vanadium a classic classroom demonstration of redox chemistry.

facts.title: The Secret In Strong Steel
facts.text: Roughly 85 percent of all vanadium produced goes into steel alloys, where adding less than one percent dramatically increases strength, toughness, and resistance to fatigue. Henry Ford famously used vanadium steel in the chassis of the Model T to make it lighter yet more durable. Vanadium steel is also prized for surgical instruments, springs, and high-speed tools.

facts.title: It Made Pure Aluminum Possible
facts.text: In 1908, American metallurgist John Wesley Marden produced metallic vanadium that was 99.7 percent pure by reducing vanadium oxide with calcium. High-purity vanadium is ductile and workable. Today vanadium is added in tiny amounts to refine the grain structure of aluminum and titanium alloys used in aerospace.

facts.title: Sea Creatures Hoard It
facts.text: Marine animals called tunicates, or sea squirts, concentrate vanadium in special blood cells called vanadocytes at levels up to a million times higher than the surrounding seawater. Scientists still debate exactly why, with theories ranging from predator defense to a role in oxygen transport. Certain mushrooms, like Amanita muscaria, also accumulate surprising amounts of vanadium.

facts.title: A Battery The Size Of A House
facts.text: Vanadium redox flow batteries store energy by dissolving vanadium ions in tanks of liquid electrolyte, exploiting the metal's multiple oxidation states. Because you can scale storage simply by using bigger tanks, these batteries are ideal for grid-scale storage of solar and wind power. The largest, in Dalian, China, can deliver hundreds of megawatt-hours.

facts.title: Possibly An Essential Nutrient
facts.text: Trace amounts of vanadium are present in the human body, and some marine and bacterial enzymes, such as vanadium-dependent nitrogenase and bromoperoxidase, rely on it to function. Studies suggest vanadium compounds can mimic insulin and lower blood sugar in animals, though they are not yet an approved human treatment. Whether vanadium is truly essential for people remains an open scientific question.

facts.title: Forged Inside Dying Stars
facts.text: Vanadium is created in the cosmos largely during supernova explosions and explosive silicon burning in massive stars. Its single stable isotope, vanadium-51, makes up about 99.75 percent of natural vanadium. The remaining trace is vanadium-50, which is faintly radioactive with a half-life of around 271 quadrillion years, far longer than the current age of the universe.

facts.title: A Catalyst For Modern Industry
facts.text: Vanadium pentoxide is the workhorse catalyst in the contact process, which manufactures sulfuric acid, one of the most produced industrial chemicals on Earth. It speeds the conversion of sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide without being consumed. The same compound also catalyzes the production of maleic anhydride, used in making plastics and resins.
